motion: Does the God of the Bible exist?

bridges.description: Positive reasons offered for the existence of the biblical God.
Observed functional complexity is traced to an intelligent designer identified with the biblical God.
Objective moral duties are traced to a standard grounded in God's nature.
Biblical coherence, prophecy, and the resurrection identify the designer and moral ground as the biblical God.
Reasons offered for concluding that the biblical God does not exist.
Mutually incompatible attributed properties are presented as ruling out the biblical God's existence.
Natural accounts of complexity and morality are offered in place of divine explanation.
Challenges to biblical reliability and Christian historical claims undercut identification of a real biblical God.

sections.title: Existence claim and definition
sections.rationale: The debate distinguishes general probability from the claimed certainty of the biblical-God question and tests whether the proposed nonmaterial being is coherently defined.

sections.title: Design and natural explanation
sections.rationale: Butt's positive design inference and Barker's naturalistic objection form a central exchange about whether observed complexity supports a designer.

sections.title: Morality and human value
sections.rationale: The speakers contest objective moral grounding, natural altruism, and distinctive human value.

sections.title: Biblical coherence and reliability
sections.rationale: Alleged contradictions, contextual answers, interpretation, and scriptural reliability directly affect the specifically biblical identification.

sections.title: Divine agency and character
sections.rationale: Foreknowledge, created agency, hell, and the moral standard attributed to God test the coherence and character of the proposed deity.

sections.title: History and salvation claims
sections.rationale: Falsifiability, Jesus, resurrection, and salvation claims connect the biblical-God case to asserted history.

sections.title: Situational moral cases
sections.rationale: The cross-examination tests harm-minimization through an extreme forced choice, a Nazi-doctor example, Barker's shared-law answer, and Butt's consistency follow-up.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: General arguments leave gods highly improbable, while the specifically described biblical God can be rejected with certainty if its properties are incompatible.
moves.warrant: Barker distinguishes probabilistic arguments about gods generally from a definitional contradiction argument about the biblical God.
moves.inference: The debate can move from evidential probability to claimed certainty when the target is the Bible's particular description.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This focused passage preserves Barker's qualification that general atheism is probabilistic, then states why he treats the specifically biblical God as a certainty question.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we can make it a question of certainty
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker opening after the moderator assigns him the con proposition.
moves.importanceRationale: It defines Barker's burden and organizing inference for the whole con case.

burdenContact.rationale: Directly states why Barker claims the biblical God does not exist.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The Bible attributes incompatible constancy, conduct, and moral qualities to God.
moves.warrant: Barker contrasts passages saying God does not change, does not punish children for parents, and is good with passages he reads as repentance, inherited punishment, and creating evil.
moves.inference: A being defined by incompatible properties resembles a married bachelor and cannot exist as described.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The contiguous passage gives the first representative clusters of Barker's contradiction case and its recurring inference.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the god of the Bible is good the god of the Bible is not good
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker opening with no speaker transition.
moves.importanceRationale: Representative textual contradictions are a principal con route against the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: Alleged incompatible divine properties directly instantiate the incoherence bridge.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Jesus' statements that his own record is both true and not true appear contradictory.
moves.warrant: Barker places the two self-testimony statements side by side.
moves.inference: The biblical witness claim is internally inconsistent.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the smallest complete passage containing both statements and Barker's contradiction inference.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: he contradicted himself
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It becomes the actual target of Butt's detailed legal-context answer.

burdenContact.rationale: It alleges a direct contradiction in the biblical portrayal of Jesus.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Exhaustive foreknowledge of God's own future actions is incompatible with open alternatives required for free personal agency.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that if God already knows every future decision, God cannot change it without prior knowledge being false.
moves.inference: The biblical God cannot simultaneously be a free personal being and omniscient about the future.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Barker's foreknowledge point and retains the complete free-agency inference through his opening conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if he does change what he's going to do then he uh was not omniscient
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker opening.
moves.importanceRationale: The foreknowledge/free-agency argument bears directly on the coherence of the biblical God's personhood.

burdenContact.rationale: It alleges contradictions within properties essential to the proposed God.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Functional design in artifacts and the still greater organized computing capacity of the human brain warrant inference to an intelligent designer.
moves.warrant: Butt first establishes the laptop as a known product of intelligence, then compares its functional computing complexity with the much greater capacity of the human brain.
moves.inference: If the lesser computing system warrants a designer inference, the human brain does as well.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span must retain both halves of Butt's analogy: events 599-644 establish why functional laptop complexity signals intelligence, and events 657-704 apply that comparison to the human brain and draw the human-design inference. Removing either half leaves only an artifact truism or an unsupported biological conclusion; intervening audience-size and six-year-old framing remains part of the contiguous delivered application.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: when you see design in the material world it Demands a designer
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt opening after his formal handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: This is one of Butt's two expressly identified primary positive arguments.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the main inferential bridge from observed complexity to a designer.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Objective moral standards require a ground beyond human preferences.
moves.warrant: Butt argues that genuinely right and wrong acts cannot be grounded in shifting individual impulses or evolutionary atheism.
moves.inference: If objective morality exists, there must be a God in whom it is grounded.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The focused span states objective right and wrong, the requirement of a standard beyond human preference, and the inference to God.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if there are objective moral standards true right and true wrong then there must be a God
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Butt's second expressly identified primary positive argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly connects objective morality to God.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Butt argues that atheistic naturalism cannot secure objective moral limits or distinctive human value.
moves.warrant: He first invokes Provine and Darwin on ethics and impulses, then uses Nazi conduct, Singer's comparison of humans and animals, and Barker's description of humans as parts of nature as applications.
moves.inference: A naturalistic account weakens the basis for distinctive human worth.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves the complete chain Butt later has to defend: the naturalism-to-impulse premise at events 737-756, the Nazi/Darwin application at 757-770, and the Singer/Barker human-value application at 771-804. These are the actual targets of Barker's rebuttal and Butt's later correction, so none can be dropped without breaking the reply structure.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's no morally different between killing a dog a pig or a human
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt opening; the eligible excerpt is explicitly Butt's report of Singer's position, not Butt's own endorsement.
moves.importanceRationale: It develops the stakes of the moral-grounding route beyond the basic syllogism.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the rival worldview lacks the moral ground Butt says God provides.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The design argument either generates a regress of designers or assumes the very complexity it seeks to explain.
moves.warrant: Barker applies the designer requirement to God's mind and contrasts that regress with observed emergence of complexity from simpler processes through natural selection.
moves.inference: Complexity does not establish a supernatural intelligent designer.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span includes the designer-regress objection, Barker's observed-complexity alternative, natural selection as the designer, and the conclusion that creationism assumes the complexity it invokes.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: in nature complexity arises from Simplicity
moves.attributionRationale: Moderator hands the rebuttal to Barker; the passage is uninterrupted.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the direct principal reply to Butt's main design argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers natural emergence as an alternative to divine design.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the move from functional complexity to an intelligent designer and supplies a natural mechanism.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Values are functions of minds and organisms, but choices can still be objectively justified by their effects on survival, flourishing, and harm.
moves.warrant: Barker distinguishes mind-independent objective values from evidence-based justification of actions and describes choosing the path of least harm.
moves.inference: Moral reasoning need not appeal to a divine, mind-independent standard.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves Barker's full distinction between objective values and objectively justified choices, including his harm criterion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we make values based upon what we need to survive
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is his central answer to Butt's moral-grounding argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives a naturalistic account of value and moral decision-making.

responseComponents.description: Rejects mind-independent values while preserving justified moral judgments.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Butt misconstrues Singer's point as devaluing humans and incorrectly labels Hitler an atheistic communist.
moves.warrant: Barker says Singer argues for extending concern to animals, then distinguishes Nazism from communism and points to Hitler's religious language and church membership.
moves.inference: These examples do not establish that atheism removes human worth or caused Nazi crimes.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The focused rebuttal contains both corrections to the examples Butt used for his moral-value claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Peter Singer is arguing not against human rights he's arguing for animal rights
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers prominent examples used to support Butt's naturalism-and-value claim.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the rival naturalistic moral position against Butt's applications.

responseComponents.description: Disputes Butt's interpretations of Singer and Hitler as evidence against atheistic morality.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Barker maintains that his contradiction examples are contextual and that the Bible contains errors and morally troubling portrayals.
moves.warrant: He asserts study of the texts, lists historical and contradictory defects, and reads Psalm 137 as celebrating violence against children.
moves.inference: Scripture is not a reliable source for establishing the biblical God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This focused rebuttal preserves Barker's reliability claim and the Psalm 137 allegation that Butt later answers.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Bible is not a reliable source of Truth
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers Butt's appeal to widespread persuasion and reasserts the reliability challenge.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly challenges scripture as a trustworthy route to the biblical God.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the leap from general design claims to the specifically biblical God by attacking scripture's reliability.
Challenges the Bible's moral portrayal as support for divine grounding.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A system that threatens eternal torture is morally bankrupt and does not merit worship.
moves.warrant: Barker characterizes hell as a threat of violence that frightens children and conditions his opposition on such a God existing.
moves.inference: The biblical hell doctrine counts against the moral character attributed to God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This focused passage preserves Barker's conditional stance, the threat-of-violence reason, and his moral conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it is a morally bankrupt system
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the retained formal argument that Butt explicitly answers in his closing.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges compatibility between divine goodness and eternal punishment.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Human morality can arise from evolved compassion and reciprocal altruism without divine commandments.
moves.warrant: Barker points to natural instincts, scientific accounts of reciprocal altruism, behavior in other species, and ordinary human moral understanding.
moves.inference: A naturalistic account can explain moral capacities without God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage preserves Barker's natural-instinct qualification, reciprocal-altruism reason, and conclusion that humans can know morality without commandments.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: human beings we know what it means to be moral without consulting some Ten Commandments
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Barker rebuttal through the final substantive words before the handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a substantial naturalistic alternative that Butt answers immediately.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers evolved social capacities as an alternative source of moral behavior.

responseComponents.description: Offers natural moral capacities as an alternative to divine grounding.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: The proposed naturalistic explanation of altruism remains uncertain.
moves.warrant: Butt quotes Matt Ridley's admission that he cannot be confident many ideas in his book are correct.
moves.inference: That account has not established a sufficient natural explanation of morality.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Butt's complete immediate reply to Barker's altruism argument, including the cited uncertainty and Butt's conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I can't even be confident that many of the ideas I discuss in this book are right
moves.attributionRationale: Moderator hands rebuttal to Butt; Butt explicitly identifies Barker's preceding altruism claim.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the direct retained answer to Barker's natural-altruism move.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the naturalistic rival has not displaced divine moral grounding.

responseComponents.description: Uses Ridley's uncertainty to challenge the completeness of the naturalistic altruism account.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: After retracting the false 'Nazi communist' wording, Butt maintains that Hitler was anti-Christian and that Singer's position can devalue newborn human life.
moves.warrant: Butt expressly corrects his error, quotes anti-Christian Table Talk passages, and quotes Singer on the moral boundary at birth.
moves.inference: Barker's corrections do not remove Butt's broader challenge about naturalism and human value.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The complete passage includes Butt's explicit correction, revised Hitler claim, and direct answer concerning Singer.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I did mess up there and say false statement about about Hitler
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves Butt's correction and the qualified form of his continuing moral-value argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends his moral-grounding route while correcting an erroneous example.

responseComponents.description: Accepts one correction, contests the Christian characterization, and offers a different Singer passage.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Jesus' apparently conflicting statements about his own testimony use 'true' in the legal sense of sufficient corroboration, not factual truth.
moves.warrant: Butt invokes the two-witness rule and distinguishes a true statement from testimony legally sufficient to establish a claim.
moves.inference: The cited verses need not contradict each other.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete explanation supplies the legal context and applies it to both statements.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the testimony of one witness although it may be true was not valid testimony
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt rebuttal with clear quotation ownership.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Butt's detailed representative answer to Barker's central contradiction method.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends coherent reading of scripture used to identify the biblical God.

responseComponents.description: Explains the apparently conflicting testimony verses through the two-witness legal context.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Psalm 137 predicts Babylon's fate rather than commanding or endorsing the killing of children.
moves.warrant: Butt reads the statement as a prediction about Persian violence and interprets 'happy' as transient prosperity rather than moral approval.
moves.inference: The passage does not support the claim that the biblical God commands the act.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the disputed verse, Butt's predictive reading, and his semantic explanation of 'happy.'
quoteEligibleExactSpans: this is a predicted statement he's talking about Babylon
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers a specific morally load-bearing textual allegation.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends scripture against a moral incoherence charge.

responseComponents.description: Answers Barker's Psalm 137 moral charge with a predictive, nonendorsing interpretation.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: The cause of material design need not share the material world's causal conditions.
moves.warrant: Butt defines God as a supernatural, eternal, uncaused, nonnatural being and argues that refusing a designer because the designer needs explanation does not erase the observed design.
moves.inference: Barker's regress objection does not defeat the inference to a designer.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage fully answers the regress objection before shifting to cosmology.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God is the first uncaused Eternal all powerful all knowing nonnatural being
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Butt's central response to Barker's strongest objection to design.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the designer inference by distinguishing material effects from a nonmaterial cause.

responseComponents.description: Rejects applying the material designer requirement to a supernatural uncaused being.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Naturalism also reaches an origin where present natural laws or ordinary causal explanation do not apply.
moves.warrant: Butt invokes Big Bang singularity discussions and contrasts an uncaused God with matter or nothing as an uncaused source.
moves.inference: Demanding a cause for God while allowing an uncaused natural origin applies the explanatory demand unevenly.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This self-contained segment states the cosmological comparison and its concluding parallel.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: matter made everything and nothing made matter
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Butt rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It broadens the response to the regress and origin challenge.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that a naturalistic origin does not have an explanatory advantage over an uncaused God.

responseComponents.description: Counters that naturalism likewise terminates explanation in an uncaused origin.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The claim that God is spirit requires a positive account of what spirit is.
moves.warrant: Barker asks Butt to move beyond the labels nonphysical and incorporeal to identify what kind of thing is asserted.
moves.inference: A clear definition is needed before the existence claim can be assessed.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Barker's initial question, Butt's brief answer, and Barker's focused request for a positive definition.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: positively what is spirit
moves.attributionRationale: Barker is the identified questioner; his challenges are separated from Butt's intervening answers by content and turn structure.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly challenges the intelligibility of the being asserted in the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges whether the being in the motion has been adequately defined.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Spirit can be described as a nonphysical ultimate mind, and incomplete knowledge of its nature does not establish atheism.
moves.warrant: Butt compares negative descriptions such as darkness and cold and argues that ignorance of exact spiritual composition is being used as an atheism-of-the-gaps inference.
moves.inference: A partial or negative description can still identify the kind of being asserted.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Butt's full analogy and his answer that lack of exhaustive definition does not entail atheism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we're inserting Atheism in a gap of human knowledge
moves.attributionRationale: This is Butt's answer in Barker-led cross-examination.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the direct pro answer to the positive-definition challenge.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends the intelligibility of the nonmaterial being asserted.

responseComponents.description: Answers that exhaustive positive composition is unnecessary and rejects an inference from incomplete definition to atheism.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: An absence-based description still leaves spirit undefined as a positive entity.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that cold and darkness name absences and that treating spirit similarly risks reducing God to nothing.
moves.inference: Butt's analogy does not supply a coherent positive definition.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This begins with Barker's response to Butt's analogy and ends with his complete conclusion that discussion requires definition.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if you can't Define it how can we even discuss whether this thing exists
moves.attributionRationale: Barker resumes questioning after Butt's answer.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Barker's direct follow-up to Butt's negative-description answer.

burdenContact.rationale: It maintains that the existence claim lacks a coherent object.

responseComponents.description: Argues that the absence analogies fail to provide a positive definition.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The biblical-God hypothesis should specify what evidence would prove it wrong.
moves.warrant: Barker explains falsifiability with the example of a black polar bear refuting a universal claim and asks for an analogous condition.
moves.inference: An existence claim insulated from possible defeat would lack a needed test.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The focused span contains Barker's falsifiability principle, example, and direct question.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: what would prove you wrong
moves.attributionRationale: Barker asks the question in his cross-examination turn.
moves.importanceRationale: It elicits Butt's historical resurrection condition.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks for a test of the specifically biblical claim.

moves.speaker: Kyle Butt
moves.claim: Christian belief would fail if Jesus did not live, die, and rise on the third day.
moves.warrant: Asked what could falsify his view, Butt names the historical existence and resurrection of Jesus as indispensable conditions.
moves.inference: The biblical-God claim is tied to historical claims that are in principle open to defeat.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The cross-examination segment contains Barker's falsifiability question and Butt's complete stated condition, ending before Barker's new historical assertion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: do you need a falsifiability statement for certain things absolutely
moves.attributionRationale: Butt's answer follows Barker's clearly marked question in Barker-led cross-examination.
moves.importanceRationale: It identifies the historical hinge of Butt's specifically Christian case.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A perfect creation requires explanation for Eve's wrong choice.
moves.warrant: After Butt affirms that creation had no flaws, Barker asks why Eve nevertheless sinned.
moves.inference: The origin of wrong choice presents a tension for perfect creation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Barker's Eve question, Butt's initial affirmation, and Barker's concise perfection challenge.

moves.claim: Eve's perfection consisted in a flawless capacity to choose, not an inability to choose wrongly.
moves.warrant: Butt compares a sound car driven off a cliff and distinguishes the created capacity from the agent's use of it.
moves.inference: A wrong choice does not show a defect in what God created.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Butt's capacity answer does not explain the source of Eve's wrong impulse.
moves.warrant: Barker argues that Eve did not create herself and that a perfect creator produced the nature from which the wrong choice arose.
moves.inference: A perfect creator producing an imperfect disposition is internally problematic.

moves.attributionRationale: Barker asks the questions and states the final inference; Butt's intervening answer is distinguishable.
moves.importanceRationale: It applies Barker's incoherence strategy to creation and agency.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: In an extremely improbable forced choice, morality may require a horrible and regrettable act if it is the only way to prevent vastly greater harm.
moves.warrant: Barker repeatedly conditions the answer on there being no alternative, describes the act as horrible, and compares it with causing limited harm for a life-saving injection.
moves.inference: Situational harm minimization can yield moral duties without treating the harmful act as intrinsically desirable.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The full passage is necessary to retain the extreme hypothetical, only-option condition, regret, improbability, and lesser-harm analogy.

burdenContact.rationale: It clarifies how Barker's nondivine moral standard handles conflicts.

moves.warrant: Butt asks whether a Nazi doctor who described Jews as a diseased appendix and claimed to protect humanity was moral merely because he intended to minimize harm.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: The four-move total difference follows the source's distinct con challenges rather than a symmetry target. Existence-definition requires Barker's burden-setting distinction, initial question, and post-answer follow-up around Butt's single answer. Design contains Butt's initial artifact-to-brain inference, two different regress/origin answers, and independent closing eye assertion against Barker's single formal natural-selection rebuttal. Divine agency contains separate con arguments from foreknowledge, hell, the initial Eve question, and the post-answer created-impulse follow-up; Butt answers Eve and hell but gives no retained formal answer to foreknowledge. History contains Barker's falsifiability question, later source corrections, resurrection/Jesus qualification, and salvation critique, while Butt's historical reply is his resurrection condition. No move is added or removed merely to equalize counts.
